title: AIP-C01 Skill 1.4.2: Add Metadata to Sharpen Retrieval
html:
AIP-C01 Skill 1.4.2: Add Metadata to Sharpen Retrieval

A hands-on lab with S3 object metadata, tags and Bedrock Knowledge Bases metadata filters. Task 1.4, post 2 of 6.

[IMAGE: cover-1-4-2.png — alt: "Skill 1.4.2: Metadata for precise retrieval"]

AIP-C01 Hands-on Labs · Domain 1 · Task 1.4: Design and implement vector store solutions · Post 2 of 6. Hands-on lab, about 45 minutes.

A customer asks how long they have to return a hedge trimmer. Your knowledge base holds last year's returns policy, this year's, and the UK one. All three are about returns, so all three are close in meaning to the question, and the model may quote the wrong one. Better embeddings won't fix that. Metadata will: if every chunk knows its region and publication date, retrieval can be told to use only the current US policy.

What AWS says

Skill 1.4.2: Develop comprehensive metadata frameworks to improve search precision and context awareness for FM interactions (for example, by using S3 object metadata for document timestamps, custom attributes for authorship information, tagging systems for domain classification).

What it means in plain words

  • Metadata framework: an agreed set of fields every document carries (who wrote it, when, which domain and region it belongs to), set automatically, not by hand.
  • S3 object metadata for timestamps: S3 records LastModified for every object, and publishers can add their own user metadata such as x-amz-meta-published.
  • Custom attributes for authorship: fields like author that travel with each chunk and can be shown with the answer.
  • Tagging for domain classification: S3 object tags such as domain=returns and region=US.

The catch: a Bedrock knowledge base doesn't read S3 user metadata or tags. It reads a small JSON file next to each document, <file>.metadata.json. The lab builds those files from S3 so nobody writes them by hand.

[IMAGE: t1-4-2-metadata-flow.png — alt: "From S3 metadata to filtered retrieval: user metadata, object tags, metadata file, typed attributes, retrieval filter, citations"]

What we're going to do

  1. Upload five short policy documents to S3 with user metadata (author, published date) and tags (domain, region).
  2. Create a knowledge base, aip-lab-kb, with an Amazon S3 Vectors store.
  3. Turn each object's S3 metadata and tags into a .metadata.json file, then sync.
  4. Ask the same question three ways: no filter, filtered to current US returns documents, and filtered by date.

What you'll learn

  • Which metadata a knowledge base can use, and where it has to be.
  • Why dates should be stored as numbers.
  • How retrieval filters work, and why they're stronger than prompt instructions.
  • How to show source, author and date with an answer.

What you'll need

  • Time and cost: about 45 minutes (mostly waiting for the knowledge base), under US$0.10
  • Region: us-west-2
  • Access: Python 3.10+ with boto3; an S3 bucket in us-west-2; permission to create a Bedrock knowledge base; access to Titan Text Embeddings V2
  • Files: github.com/prasanth2006z/aip-c01-labs, folder domain-1/task-1.4/skill-1.4.2-metadata

This lab creates the knowledge base that the Skill 1.4.4 and 1.4.5 labs reuse. Keep it until you finish Task 1.4.

The lab

Step 1: Upload the documents with metadata and tags

pip install boto3
export LAB_BUCKET=your-bucket-name
python metadata_lab.py upload

Each document is uploaded the way its owner would publish it: user metadata for authorship and date, tags for classification.

s3.put_object(Bucket=BUCKET, Key=PREFIX + name, Body=body,
              Metadata={"author": "returns-team", "published": "2026-02-01"},
              Tagging="domain=returns&region=US")

The five files are two versions of the US returns policy (2025 and 2026), a UK returns policy, a power tool warranty page and a shipping page.

Step 2: Create the knowledge base

In the Amazon Bedrock console, open Knowledge Bases → Create → Knowledge Base with vector store:

  • Name: aip-lab-kb, with a new service role
  • Data source: Amazon S3, s3://your-bucket-name/kb-docs/; default parsing and chunking
  • Embeddings model: Titan Text Embeddings V2
  • Vector store: Quick create a new vector store → Amazon S3 Vectors

Don't sync yet. Copy the knowledge base ID and data source ID:

export KB_ID=XXXXXXXXXX DS_ID=XXXXXXXXXX

Step 3: Build the metadata files

python metadata_lab.py sidecars

For each document the script reads its user metadata and tags from S3 and writes returns-policy-2026.txt.metadata.json beside it:

{"metadataAttributes": {
  "domain": "returns", "region": "US", "author": "returns-team",
  "published_year": 2026, "published": 20260201, "last_modified": "2026-..."
}}

Notice the dates. published is stored as the number 20260201, not the string "2026-02-01". Range filters (greaterThan, lessThan) work on numbers, so a date you want to filter by must be a number.

In production this script would be a Lambda function triggered by each S3 upload, so the metadata file is always written with the document.

Step 4: Sync

python metadata_lab.py sync

The sync chunks and embeds each document and attaches its metadata attributes to every chunk. The statistics should show five documents indexed (metadata files are not counted as documents).

Step 5: Ask with and without filters

python metadata_lab.py ask

The question is “How long do I have to return a hedge trimmer?”, asked three times:

  • No filter: a mix. The 2025 and 2026 US policies and the UK policy all score well, because all three talk about returns.
  • Current US returns only: only the 2026 US policy (14 days for hedge trimmers).
{"andAll": [
    {"equals": {"key": "domain", "value": "returns"}},
    {"equals": {"key": "region", "value": "US"}},
    {"greaterThanOrEquals": {"key": "published_year", "value": 2026}},
]}
  • Published after 1 March 2026: only the warranty page. Its text is a weaker match for the question, but it's the only document that passes the filter.

That third result is the lesson: a filter is a hard rule applied during the search, not a hint. Only chunks that match ever reach the model. A prompt saying “use only the latest policy” can't do that, because the model never sees which document is newer unless you tell it.

Step 6: Show where the answer came from

Each retrieval result carries its metadata, so the application can print the source, author and date beside the answer. The same metadata appears in the citations of RetrieveAndGenerate. Users trust an answer more when they can see it came from the 2026 policy.

Common pitfalls

  • Filters return nothing: keys and values are case-sensitive (US is not us), and the metadata file must be named exactly <document name>.metadata.json in the same folder.
  • Date filter ignored or failing: the attribute is a string. Store dates as numbers such as 20260201.
  • Metadata changed but results didn't: metadata is read during sync. Sync again after changing a metadata file.
  • Expecting tags to work by themselves: the knowledge base doesn't read S3 tags or user metadata; only the metadata file.

Clean up

Keep the knowledge base, bucket and IDs: the next two labs use them. When you finish Task 1.4, the task README in the repo lists everything to delete (the knowledge base, its S3 vector bucket and index, the service role and the kb-docs/ objects).

What to remember

  • Knowledge Bases read metadata from <file>.metadata.json next to each S3 document, not from S3 tags or user metadata.
  • Derive those files automatically from what publishers already set: user metadata, tags and LastModified.
  • Store dates as numbers so range filters work.
  • Filters (equals, greaterThan, andAll, orAll) are hard rules applied during retrieval.
  • “Answers quote an old or wrong-region document” is a metadata problem, not a model problem.

The exam scenarios for this skill are in post 6 of this task: Task 1.4 Exam Notes.

References
